Reference: Masters R, Anwar E, Collins B, Cookson R, Capewell S (2017). Return on investment of public health interventions: a systematic review. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health 71(8):827-834
Task described: Quantifies the economic return of public health interventions, to make the case for spending on prevention
Metrics / indicators: Return on investment (how many dollars come back per dollar spent); cost-benefit ratio
Geographic level: National and local, depending on the intervention
Input data: 52 studies included from 2,957 titles screened across seven research databases
Output: Pooled return-on-investment estimates: median 14.3 to 1 overall; 4.1 to 1 for local interventions; 27.2 to 1 for national ones
Data sources used: Published intervention cost and outcome data from the included studies
Public data sources?: Not a dataset - a review of published studies. The papers themselves are published

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2026). Potentially preventable hospitalisations in Australia by small geographic areas: 2017-18 to 2023-24. Web report, catalogue number HPF 76
Task described: National monitoring of hospital admissions that could have been avoided through timely care in the community - the standard system-level indicator, and the natural benchmark for judging whether prevention is shifting hospital demand
Metrics / indicators: Potentially preventable hospitalisation rate per 100,000 people, adjusted for age; split into acute, chronic and vaccine-preventable groups
Geographic level: Statistical Area Level 3 (346 small areas of about 30,000-130,000 people); also Primary Health Network (33 of them), remoteness (4 categories) and socioeconomic quintile (5 groups from most to least disadvantaged)
Input data: Records of admitted hospital patients across seven financial years, 2017-18 to 2023-24
Output: Counts and rates for 22 preventable conditions. In 2023-24, 778,133 hospitalisations were potentially preventable - 6.2% of all 12.6 million hospitalisations - using 3.07 million bed days, average stay 3.9 days
Data sources used: National Hospital Morbidity Database; population estimates from the Australian Bureau of Statistics
Public data sources?: Yes - Excel and CSV are free to download. Patient-level hospital records remain restricted
Scale:
868,000 rows covering 7 financial years (2017-18 to 2023-24).
Covers 346 small areas, 33 Primary Health Networks, 4 remoteness categories, and 5 disadvantage quintiles.
Key attributes: Splits by year, area, sex, age (under 65 and 65 plus), condition (22 of them) and category (acute, chronic, vaccine-preventable). Measures: number of admissions, rate per 100,000, bed days, and average length of stay

Reference: Falster MO, Jorm LR, Douglas KA, Blyth FM, Elliott RF, Leyland AH (2015). Sociodemographic and health characteristics, rather than primary care supply, are major drivers of geographic variation in preventable hospitalizations in Australia. Medical Care 53(5):436-445
Task described: An important caution for this topic: it works out why preventable hospitalisation rates differ between areas, and finds the answer is mostly who lives there, not how many services are available. Guards against over-crediting or over-blaming local programs
Metrics / indicators: Share of the between-area difference explained: general practitioner supply 2.9%, versus people's own social and health characteristics 36.9%
Geographic level: Statistical Local Area (199 areas across New South Wales)
Input data: 267,091 people surveyed in the 45 and Up Study (262,755 analysed after exclusions), linked to New South Wales hospital and death records; plus general practitioner supply across 199 small areas
Output: General practitioner supply was NOT a significant predictor of preventable hospitalisation
Data sources used: 45 and Up Study survey; New South Wales Admitted Patient Data Collection; death records; general practitioner workforce data
Public data sources?: No - survey and hospital records need application
Key attributes: Per person: age, sex, income, education, smoking, physical activity, body mass index, long-term conditions. Per area: number of general practitioners. Outcome: preventable admissions

Reference: Jorm LR, Leyland AH, Blyth FM, Elliott RF, Douglas KMA, Redman S, on behalf of the APHID Investigators (2012). Assessing Preventable Hospitalisation InDicators (APHID): protocol for a data-linkage study using cohort study and administrative data. BMJ Open 2:e002344
Task described: Sets out how to test what actually drives preventable hospitalisation at the level of individual people - the evidence chain this topic needs
Metrics / indicators: Planned comparisons of preventable hospitalisation rates by health behaviour and social background
Geographic level: Individual people, New South Wales
Input data: The 45 and Up Study group of participants, linked to hospital, death and Medicare records
Output: Study design and analysis plan for checking the preventable hospitalisation indicator against individual characteristics
Data sources used: 45 and Up Study survey; New South Wales Admitted Patient Data Collection; Medicare and pharmaceutical records; death registry, joined together by the Centre for Health Record Linkage

Reference: Vos T, Carter R, Barendregt J, Mihalopoulos C, Veerman L, Magnus A, Cobiac L, Bertram M, Wallace A (2010). Assessing Cost-Effectiveness in Prevention (ACE-Prevention): Final Report. University of Queensland & Deakin University
Task described: Ranks preventive interventions by value for money - the landmark Australian exercise in deciding which prevention to fund first, led by the University of Queensland
Metrics / indicators: Cost per healthy year of life gained (measured as disability-adjusted life years averted); savings elsewhere in the health system
Geographic level: National
Input data: Disease data, effect sizes and costs for 123 preventive and 27 treatment interventions
Output: A ranked table of interventions showing which prevention gives the best value; tax and regulatory measures came out strongest
Data sources used: Australian burden of disease data; national health and population statistics; published trial evidence
Public data sources?: Not a dataset - the underlying models were not released

Reference: World Health Organization (2018). Saving lives, spending less: a strategic response to noncommunicable diseases. Geneva: World Health Organization
Task described: The investment case for preventing chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes - the large-scale version of this topic's question
Metrics / indicators: Return on investment per intervention; deaths avoided; healthy years of life gained
Geographic level: National (modelled across many countries)
Input data: Disease and cost data by country for the World Health Organization's recommended 'best buy' interventions
Output: Projected returns: every US$1 invested returns US$7 by 2030 in lower-income countries
Data sources used: World Health Organization global health estimates; country-level costing

Reference: Owen L, Morgan A, Fischer A, Ellis S, Hoy A, Kelly MP (2012). The cost-effectiveness of public health interventions. Journal of Public Health 34(1):37-45
Task described: Shows that most public health interventions assessed for England's national clinical guidance are highly cost-effective - a counter to the claim that prevention does not pay off
Metrics / indicators: Cost per quality-adjusted life year (a year of life weighted by health status)
Geographic level: National (England)
Input data: 21 economic analyses that underpinned national public health guidance issued between 2006 and 2010
Output: Most results fell well within what the health system treats as good value; many interventions saved money outright
Data sources used: Economic models built on English cost and disease data
Public data sources?: No single dataset. 200 estimates are available in the paper itself

Reference: Purdy S (2010). Avoiding hospital admissions: what does the research evidence say? London: The King's Fund
Task described: Reviews which interventions genuinely reduce unplanned hospital admissions - a useful reality-check on the claims made about this topic
Metrics / indicators: Emergency and unplanned admission rates; admissions for conditions treatable outside hospital
Geographic level: National and local (England)
Input data: Published evaluations of programs intended to avoid hospital admissions
Output: Grades the evidence: some approaches work, while several widely used ones have weak or no supporting evidence
Data sources used: English hospital activity statistics used in the underlying studies

Reference: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (2023). Health at a Glance 2023: OECD Indicators. Paris: OECD Publishing
Task described: International benchmarking of avoidable admissions - places Australia alongside comparable health systems
Metrics / indicators: Admissions per 100,000 people, adjusted for age and sex
Geographic level: National
Input data: National hospital discharge data submitted by member countries
Output: Country-by-country comparison of avoidable admission rates for asthma, chronic lung disease, heart failure and diabetes
Data sources used: OECD health statistics database
Public data sources?: Yes - free from the OECD portal
Scale: 38 member countries plus selected partners

Reference: Harriss LR, Thompson F, Lawson K, O'Loughlin M, McDermott R (2019). Preventable hospitalisations in regional Queensland: potential for primary health? Australian Health Review 43(4):371-381
Task described: A Queensland-specific analysis - the most locally relevant evidence in this table for where prevention could reduce hospital demand
Metrics / indicators: Preventable hospitalisation rates by condition and region
Geographic level: Regional Queensland
Input data: Queensland hospital admission records for regional areas
Output: Patterns of preventable hospitalisation across regional Queensland, and the share that community-based care could address
Data sources used: Queensland Health admitted patient data
Public data sources?: No - needs application to Queensland Health
Scale: Demographic data and clinical information on all admitted patients separated from both public and licensed private hospitals and private day surgeries in Queensland

Reference: Joint Regional Needs Assessments, Queensland (series). Produced jointly by each Primary Health Network and its Hospital and Health Service, 2025-2027 cycle
Task described: Each Queensland region publishes an assessment of what its population needs and where services fall short, agreed jointly by the local Primary Health Network and hospital service. These are not datasets, but they name the priority indicators each region has settled on and say where the numbers came from - and unlike a research paper they are redone on a cycle, so they stay current. Seven Primary Health Networks means roughly seven documents. This row covers the series; Brisbane South and North Brisbane and Moreton Bay are the two linked.
Metrics / indicators: Whatever each region has prioritised - typically chronic disease, obesity, smoking, mental health, alcohol and other drugs, and potentially preventable hospitalisations
Geographic level: Primary Health Network catchment and Hospital and Health Service, broken down to Statistical Area Level 2 and 3 and local government area
Input data: Population and hospital data for the region, plus consultation with local services and community
Output: A free report per region setting out priority health needs and service gaps
Data sources used: Brisbane South cites the Queensland Preventive Health Survey, the 2021 Census through the Queensland Government Statistician's Office, Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data, Medicare claims, and Queensland Health's non-admitted patient collection
Public data sources?: Free PDFs, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia. Useful mainly as a map to other people's data: they say which indicator a region cares about and which collection it came from, which is faster than working that out from scratch.
Data sources link: Brisbane South 2025-2027: https://www.metrosouth.health.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0022/386014/brisbane-south-jrna-report-2025-2027.pdf North Brisbane and Moreton Bay 2025-27: https://metronorth.health.qld.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/jrna-summary-25-27.pdf
Scale: One report per Primary Health Network catchment; Brisbane South covers 23 per cent of Queensland's population
Key attributes: Priority health needs per region, with the source of each figure named
Topics: Health system impact; Health inequities; Regional partnerships; Prevention programs

Reference: Department of Health (2025). Health Indicators 2025: Snapshot series I. Population profiles. Metro South Health, Brisbane
Task described: A worked example of one Queensland hospital service profiling its own population down to suburb groupings, and reporting it by council area. It shows the level of detail a Queensland health service can already produce for a council-sized area, which is the question Application 6 keeps running into.
Metrics / indicators: Population and projections, growth, median age, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander share, country of birth, language, and the health indicators in the wider snapshot series
Geographic level: Hospital and Health Service, local government area (Logan, Redland and southern Brisbane), and Statistical Area Level 2 and 3
Input data: Population estimates and projections, the 2021 Census, and Queensland Health collections
Output: A free 64-page report with tables per area, including an appendix of the underlying figures
Data sources used: Australian Bureau of Statistics population estimates and the 2021 Census; Queensland Health collections
Public data sources?: Free PDF, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Australia. The report is public; the tables come as a PDF appendix rather than a data file, so anything computed from it has to be retyped. Note the report also points at an internal Queensland Health address for an electronic version, which is not reachable from outside.
Scale: 1.31 million residents, 23 per cent of Queensland, across 20 Statistical Area Level 3s and 116 Statistical Area Level 2s
Key attributes: Population and demographic profile per area, with Queensland figures alongside for comparison
Topics: Health system impact; Local government measurement

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2024). Australian Burden of Disease Study 2024. Canberra: AIHW. Catalogue number BOD 40
Task described: Puts a number on how much illness and early death each disease and each risk factor causes. The standard Australian source for arguing that preventing something is worth the spend.
Metrics / indicators: Years of healthy life lost, split into years lost to early death and years lived with illness, by disease and by risk factor
Geographic level: National only. The 2024 study publishes no state, remoteness or socioeconomic breakdowns; for those, the 2018 study is the source
Input data: Hospital, death, survey and registry collections, projected forward using historical trends
Output: Estimates for 220 diseases and injuries, and the share of burden attributable to 20 individual risk factors
Data sources used: AIHW and ABS collections
Public data sources?: Free web report, PDF and interactive data, no registration. The underlying linked collections are not released.
Scale: 220 diseases and injuries; 20 risk factors
Key attributes: The 2024 figures are projections built on historical trends rather than fresh collection, which matters when quoting them

Reference: Sallis JF, Cerin E, Conway TL, Adams MA, Frank LD, Pratt M, et al. (2016). Physical activity in relation to urban environments in 14 cities worldwide: a cross-sectional study. The Lancet 387:2207-2217
Task described: Tests whether the design of a neighbourhood actually changes how much people move, using the same measurements in every city. The strongest single piece of evidence that the built environment is worth investing in at all.
Metrics / indicators: Minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity per day, against residential density, street intersection density, public transport stop density and park count
Geographic level: The area within 0.5 to 1 kilometre of a person's home
Input data: Accelerometers worn by 6,822 adults, plus mapped features of the neighbourhood around each person's home
Output: Four environment features explained a difference of up to 89 minutes of physical activity a week between neighbourhoods
Data sources used: The International Physical Activity and Environment Network (IPEN) Adult study
Public data sources?: The paper is open access. Whether the pooled study data can be obtained is not stated on any public page - the collaboration would have to be asked.
Scale: 6,822 adults, aged 18 to 66
Key attributes: Per person: measured activity, age, sex, education. Per neighbourhood: density, street connectivity, transport stops, parks
Indicators: Street connectivity; Dwelling density; Public transport accessibility

Reference: Astell-Burt T, Feng X (2019). Urban green space, tree canopy and prevention of cardiometabolic diseases: a multilevel longitudinal study of 46,786 Australians. International Journal of Epidemiology 49(3):926-933
Task described: Follows the same people over years to see whether living near tree cover, specifically, protects against heart disease and diabetes. It separates tree canopy from grass, which matters because councils choose what to plant.
Metrics / indicators: Percentage of tree canopy and of open grass within 1.6 kilometres of home, against new diagnoses over time
Geographic level: The area within 1.6 kilometres of a person's home
Input data: A large cohort survey linked to mapped green space around each home
Output: More tree canopy was associated with lower odds of developing heart disease, high blood pressure and diabetes; open grass was not
Data sources used: The 45 and Up Study, linked to land-cover mapping
Public data sources?: The paper is open access. The 45 and Up Study data takes a formal application to the Sax Institute.
Scale: 46,786 adults followed over roughly six years
Key attributes: Tree canopy share, grass share, and incident heart disease, hypertension and diabetes per person
Indicators: Tree canopy/shade coverage; Green space access

Reference: Alderton A, O'Connor M, Badland H, Gunn L, Boulange C, Villanueva K (2022). Access to and quality of neighbourhood public open space and children's mental health outcomes: evidence from population linked data across eight Australian capital cities. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 19(11):6780
Task described: Asks whether it is having a park nearby that matters, or having a good one. The answer bears directly on whether a council should build more parks or improve the ones it has.
Metrics / indicators: Distance to public open space and its size, against teacher-reported child emotional and social development
Geographic level: Neighbourhood, across eight Australian capital cities
Input data: A national children's development census linked to mapped open space
Output: Quality mattered as well as distance - being near a large park was linked to better emotional outcomes for children
Data sources used: Australian Early Development Census, linked to open space mapping
Public data sources?: The paper is open access. The Early Development Census is published as area summaries; record-level data takes a request.
Scale: Children in their first year of full-time school, across eight capital cities
Key attributes: Open space distance and size, child development domain scores, area disadvantage
Indicators: Green space access

Reference: Needham C, Allender S, Blake MR, Horta A (2025). The influence of access to healthy food retail on BMI: implications for obesity prevention policy at the local government level. Health & Place 95:103521
Task described: The closest match in this scan to what a Queensland council could act on for healthy eating: it tests whether the mix of food outlets in a council area is linked to residents' weight, and draws out what that means for local policy.
Metrics / indicators: Counts and proportions of healthy versus unhealthy food outlets in an area, against body mass index
Geographic level: Local government area
Input data: Mapped food retail outlets by type, and measured body mass index
Output: Findings on how the local food retail mix relates to body mass index, framed for local government decisions
Data sources used: Food outlet business listings mapped geographically, and population health survey data
Public data sources?: Check the paper for access. Outlet listings are usually commercial; the health measures come from survey collections.
Scale: Australian local government areas
Key attributes: Food outlet counts by type per area, body mass index, area disadvantage
Indicators: Healthy food outlet density; Healthy food access

Reference: Sacks G, Kwon J, Vandevijvere S, Swinburn B (2021). Benchmarking as a public health strategy for creating healthy food environments: an evaluation of the INFORMAS initiative (2012-2020). Annual Review of Public Health 42:345-362
Task described: Reviews whether publishing a scorecard that ranks governments and companies on food policy actually changes what they do. Directly relevant to the benchmarking idea behind a council measurement framework.
Metrics / indicators: The INFORMAS food environment policy index and the modules underneath it - food composition, labelling, promotion, prices, provision, retail and trade
Geographic level: National, with some sub-national application
Input data: Ten years of monitoring work across the INFORMAS network
Output: An assessment of where benchmarking has shifted policy and where it has not
Data sources used: The INFORMAS monitoring modules
Public data sources?: The framework and its methods are published. Country assessments are released as reports.
Scale: A global network covering many countries
Key attributes: Policy domains scored against international best practice

Reference: Department of Transport and Main Roads. Queensland Household Travel Survey series. Brisbane: Queensland Government
Task described: Records how Queensland households actually travelled over a single day - by what means, where to and why. It is the state's own measure of active transport, and the only Queensland source here that captures walking and cycling trips directly rather than only the journey to work.
Metrics / indicators: Trips by mode including walking and cycling, trip purpose, time of day, distance and duration
Geographic level: South East Queensland and regional centres; released by travel zone and larger areas
Input data: Travel diaries from randomly approached households over a 24-hour period
Output: Downloadable trip records, released as single years and as pooled multi-year files so smaller areas have enough trips to report
Data sources used: The Queensland Household Travel Survey itself
Public data sources?: Free from the Queensland open data portal, no registration. Surveys have run in South East Queensland since 1976 and in regional centres since 1986, so there is a long back series.
Scale: Randomly sampled Queensland households, pooled across three-year windows
Key attributes: One record per trip: mode, purpose, origin and destination zone, start time, distance, duration, plus household characteristics
Indicators: Active transport mode share

Reference: Queensland Government. Queensland Globe and the Queensland Spatial Catalogue. Brisbane: Department of Resources
Task described: The state's map of itself - parks, land use, roads, vegetation and property boundaries, viewable and downloadable. It is where the physical side of a council area comes from when nobody has already turned it into an indicator.
Metrics / indicators: Not indicators as such - the underlying layers from which green space, park access and land use measures get built
Geographic level: Any, down to individual parcels
Input data: Queensland Government spatial and land administration collections
Output: An online map, and downloadable spatial layers
Data sources used: Queensland Government departmental spatial data
Public data sources?: Free to view and download, no registration. This is raw mapping rather than finished measures, so using it means someone has to compute the indicator.
Scale: All of Queensland
Key attributes: Spatial layers: land use, tenure, vegetation, protected areas, transport, addresses
Indicators: Tree canopy/shade coverage; Green space access

Reference: Queensland Government. Queensland Government Open Data Portal. Brisbane: Queensland Government
Task described: The single place Queensland agencies publish their data. Several of the sources in this scan are hosted here, and it is the first place to look before assuming a Queensland figure does not exist.
Metrics / indicators: Varies by dataset
Geographic level: Varies by dataset, from state down to address
Input data: Whatever Queensland agencies choose to publish
Output: Downloadable files and interfaces, dataset by dataset
Data sources used: Queensland Government agencies
Public data sources?: Free, no registration. Most datasets are Creative Commons Attribution. Coverage is uneven - it holds what agencies have chosen to publish, not everything they hold.
Scale: All of Queensland
Key attributes: Varies by dataset
Topics: Regional environments; Regional partnerships; Local government measurement

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics. General Social Survey, Australia. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: The national measure of how connected people are - who they can turn to, whether they feel lonely, whether they volunteer. It fills the social side of the indicator list, which nothing else in this scan measures directly.
Metrics / indicators: Social connection and support, feelings of loneliness, volunteering, community involvement, trust, and experience of discrimination
Geographic level: Australia and states and territories; not published below that
Input data: A national household survey of people aged 15 and over
Output: Published tables and summary results; detailed data through the ABS on request
Data sources used: The General Social Survey itself
Public data sources?: Summary tables are free. This is its limitation for council work: the sample is not large enough to publish below state level, so it cannot compare one council area with another.
Scale: A national household sample, run every few years
Key attributes: Social support, loneliness, volunteering, trust, community involvement, by age, sex and state
Topics: Regional environments; Regional partnerships; Health inequities
Indicators: Loneliness; Social connectedness; Volunteering rate; Community participation

Reference: Australian Early Development Census. Canberra: Australian Government Department of Education
Task described: Teachers assess every child in their first year of school on how they are doing physically, socially, emotionally and in language. Because it covers every child rather than a sample, it reports at community and council level - which almost nothing else about wellbeing does.
Metrics / indicators: Proportion of children developmentally vulnerable on each of five domains: physical health and wellbeing, social competence, emotional maturity, language and cognitive skills, and communication
Geographic level: AEDC community, local government area, state and national
Input data: A teacher-completed instrument for each child, run every three years
Output: Free community profiles and downloadable data tables by area
Data sources used: The census itself
Public data sources?: Free community profiles and data tables, no registration. Record-level data takes an application. Small communities are suppressed to protect identifiable children.
Scale: Every child in their first year of full-time school, every three years since 2009
Key attributes: Percentage developmentally vulnerable per domain, per area, over successive cycles
Topics: Regional environments; Health inequities; Local government measurement

Reference: Strava Metro. Aggregated cycling and pedestrian movement data. San Francisco: Strava, Inc. (ongoing since 2014)
Task described: Counts how many people walked or cycled along each street and path, from phone and GPS-watch recordings. Answers where active travel actually happens, which a household survey is too small to show street by street.
Metrics / indicators: Counts of walking and cycling trips per street segment over time, before-and-after comparison around infrastructure changes, and the routes people take or avoid
Geographic level: Street segment, within an area of interest chosen at the level Strava calls county, which for Australia is council-sized
Input data: Walking, running and cycling activities recorded on the Strava app, stripped of identifiers and aggregated. Activities members marked private, and those of members who deleted their accounts, are left out.
Output: A web dashboard of counts per street segment, with origin and destination patterns, and shapefile export for anyone with mapping software
Data sources used: Strava's own member activity uploads
Public data sources?: Free. Access is by application for a Metro partnership, and Strava restricts who is eligible: it works only with organisations that plan, own or maintain infrastructure or seek to positively influence planning processes, and names real estate investors, financial services and retailers as examples it will not partner with. Metro is free, but Strava does not say how much historical data a partner can access. Academics can apply separately through the Metro for Academic Researchers Program, which gives one year of access; the 2027 round closes 23 October 2026.
Scale: Millions of activities recorded each week worldwide. An Australian council, the City of Stonnington, is among the partners Strava quotes
Key attributes: One record per street segment per period. The caveat that matters is who is in it: Strava users are not a random sample of the population, so the counts show relative patterns rather than true volumes. Strava says academic studies have found the data correlates well with physical bike counters, and that partners who hold counter data adjust against it.
Indicators: Walking & cycling counts
Data source year(s): Strava does not state how far back the available data goes. Metro launched in 2014 and is operating in 2026.

Reference: Department of Transport and Main Roads. TMR Bicycle Counts. Brisbane: Queensland Government open data portal (updated quarterly)
Task described: Counts bicycles passing fixed loggers around Queensland, year by year. One of the few sources that measures active travel directly rather than asking people about it.
Metrics / indicators: Bicycle numbers per counter site over time
Geographic level: Individual counter sites across Queensland
Input data: Automated counters placed around Queensland under the Transport and Main Roads Active Transport program
Output: One CSV per year from 2018 to 2025, plus a site list and a data dictionary
Data sources used: The department's own counter network
Public data sources?: Free CSV download, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Updated quarterly.
Scale: Eight full years of counts, 2018 to 2025, across the Active Transport site list
Key attributes: Two limitations the department states itself: counts may include e-scooters and similar devices, because some counters cannot tell them from bicycles, and some sites have gaps from maintenance, faults or vandalism
Indicators: Walking & cycling counts

Reference: Brisbane City Council. Pedestrian movement counts. Brisbane: Brisbane City Council open data (updated daily)
Task described: Counts movements past sensors in Brisbane's main pedestrian precincts. The closest thing the scan holds to a live measure of foot traffic in a Queensland city centre.
Metrics / indicators: Pedestrian movements per sensor over time
Geographic level: Individual sensor locations within Brisbane
Input data: Line-breaking sensors in key economic precincts, including Queen Street Mall and Brunswick Street
Output: Counts per sensor, published through the council's open data site
Data sources used: The council's own sensor network
Public data sources?: Free, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Updated daily. The record on the Queensland portal points at the council's own site for the download and viewing tools.
Scale: Key economic precincts in Brisbane rather than the whole council area
Key attributes: Counts movements, not people: the council states the sensors detect everything crossing the line regardless of mode and cannot tell a person from an object, so a figure is not a headcount. Counts below 25 are suppressed for privacy, and values estimated during sensor or network faults are flagged in the data. Covers shopping and entertainment precincts, so it measures where people already gather rather than walking across the city.
Indicators: Walking & cycling counts

Reference: Brisbane City Council. Bikeway counts. Brisbane: Brisbane City Council open data (updated annually)
Task described: Counts bikes and pedestrians on Brisbane's bikeways, used by the council to see whether a cycleway is being ridden and to plan the next one.
Metrics / indicators: Cycleway patronage by site
Geographic level: Counter sites across the Brisbane local government area
Input data: Automated and manual bike and pedestrian counts on council bikeways
Output: Counts by site and period. The published table holds 2022 to 2025; earlier years are in downloadable attachments, and a companion dataset holds the 2004 to 2018 manual surveys
Data sources used: The council's own bikeway monitoring
Public data sources?: Free, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Updated annually, with the download on the council's own open data site.
Scale: Brisbane bikeway network, with counts going back to 2004 once the attachments are included alongside the tables
Key attributes: The council states the data is used to 'capture cycleway patronage and support bikeway plan[ning]', so it is collected to judge infrastructure rather than to represent the population
Indicators: Walking & cycling counts

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics. National Health Survey. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: The national measure of health conditions and risk factors, and the benchmark a Queensland figure gets compared against. Worth holding next to the Queensland preventive health survey: this one covers the country but stops at state level, while the Queensland one reaches council areas.
Metrics / indicators: Long-term health conditions, measured height and weight, physical activity, fruit and vegetable intake, smoking, alcohol, and psychological distress
Geographic level: Australia and states and territories
Input data: A national household survey with interviews and physical measurements
Output: Published tables and summary results; detailed microdata through the ABS on application
Data sources used: The National Health Survey itself
Public data sources?: Summary tables are free. Detailed microdata takes a DataLab or microdata application. The limitation for council work is the same as the General Social Survey - the sample does not support figures below state level.
Scale: A national household sample, run every few years
Key attributes: Condition prevalence, measured body mass index, activity, diet, smoking and distress, by age, sex and state
Topics: Prevention programs; Health system impact; Health inequities
Domain: Physical Activity; Healthy Eating; Mental Wellbeing
Indicators: Fruit intake; Vegetable intake; Adults meeting PA guidelines; Psychological distress; Self-rated health

Reference: Milat AJ, Bauman A, Redman S (2015). Narrative review of models and success factors for scaling up public health interventions. Implementation Science 10:113
Task described: Asks why prevention programs that work in a trial so often fail when rolled out widely, and what separates the ones that survive. Written from within the New South Wales health system, so the constraints it describes are the local ones.
Metrics / indicators: Not measures - the conditions to check before committing to a wider rollout
Geographic level: Not applicable
Input data: Published models and evaluations of scaled-up public health programs
Output: The factors that repeatedly decide whether a program scales: fit with existing delivery systems, cost, workforce, and political support
Data sources used: Published literature
Public data sources?: Open access paper. It is guidance rather than data.
Scale: A review of the published evidence
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Glasgow RE, Vogt TM, Boles SM (1999). Evaluating the public health impact of health promotion interventions: the RE-AIM framework. American Journal of Public Health 89(9):1322-1327
Task described: The standard way of judging a prevention program on more than whether it worked for the people who took part. It asks how many were reached, how many settings adopted it, whether it was delivered as intended, and whether it lasted - which is the gap-finding question for Application 3.
Metrics / indicators: Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation and Maintenance
Geographic level: Whatever the program covers
Input data: Program delivery and outcome records
Output: A five-part assessment that stops a program looking successful because it reached a small and willing group
Data sources used: Whatever the program collects
Public data sources?: The framework is published and freely used. It is a method, not data.
Scale: Applies to a single program
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Smith JL, Reece LJ, Rose CL, Owen KB (2022). Improving access to public physical activity events for disadvantaged communities in Australia. BMC Public Health 22:1542
Task described: Measures how far people live from the nearest free community running event, and whether that distance is longer in poorer areas. It then works out where 100 new events would do the most to close the gap. A worked example of the question this application asks, whether prevention reaches the people it should.
Metrics / indicators: Share of the population living within 5 kilometres of an event, and average distance to the nearest event, both split by area disadvantage
Geographic level: Small area, across Australia
Input data: The locations of 403 existing parkrun events, where people live, and an index of area disadvantage
Output: Average distance to the nearest event by disadvantage group, and a proposed list of 100 new locations chosen to close the gap
Data sources used: Population and area disadvantage data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, with the published list of parkrun event locations
Public data sources?: Open access paper. The inputs are population counts and the disadvantage index, both free from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, plus the public list of event locations. Note this measures how far away an event is, not how many people went.
Scale: The whole Australian population measured against 403 existing events. 63 per cent live within 5 kilometres of one; the most disadvantaged fifth average 27 kilometres away against 7 for the least.
Key attributes: Per area: population, disadvantage group, and distance to the nearest event
Data source year(s): 2016 Census areas, 2020 population, events at July 2021

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. Medicare-subsidised GP, allied health and specialist health care across local areas. Canberra: AIHW
Task described: Counts how much general practice, allied health and specialist care people in each local area actually used. This is the closest thing to a map of where primary care is thin, which is the gap question this application asks.
Metrics / indicators: Services per 100 people, patients seen, and out-of-pocket costs, by service group
Geographic level: Primary Health Network area and Statistical Area Level 3
Input data: Medicare claims for non-hospital services
Output: Downloadable tables of services and patients per area, with rates adjusted so areas can be compared
Data sources used: Medicare Benefits Schedule claims
Public data sources?: Free spreadsheets and zipped CSV files, no registration. Note it counts services claimed through Medicare, so anything delivered another way is invisible to it.
Scale: All Medicare non-hospital services nationally, updated annually
Key attributes: Service group, area, services per 100 people, patients, bulk billing and out-of-pocket cost
Topics: Prevention programs; Health system impact; Health inequities

Reference: Australian Sports Commission. AusPlay survey. Canberra: Australian Sports Commission
Task described: The national count of who plays sport and takes part in physical activity, and through what - a club, a gym, or on their own. It answers the participation half of the physical activity measures, which the preventive health survey does not break down by setting.
Metrics / indicators: Participation rates by activity, frequency, whether organised through a club, and reasons for not taking part
Geographic level: Australia, states and territories, and some larger sub-state areas
Input data: A continuous national telephone survey of adults and, through their parents, children
Output: Published tables and an online explorer, plus data on request
Data sources used: The AusPlay survey itself
Public data sources?: Results are free. Below state level the sample thins out, so council-level figures generally are not available.
Scale: A continuous national sample
Key attributes: Activity type, frequency, setting, club membership, barriers, by age, sex and area
Indicators: Club/sport membership

Reference: CQUniversity Australia. 10,000 Steps program. Rockhampton: Physical Activity Research Group, CQUniversity
Task described: A long-running Queensland physical activity program that people and workplaces log steps into. Worth knowing about because it is a prevention program with its own participation records, run from a Queensland university, rather than a survey of the population.
Metrics / indicators: Steps logged, participants registered, challenges completed
Geographic level: Wherever participants are; not a population measure
Input data: Steps logged by registered participants and workplace teams
Output: Participant dashboards and challenge results; research outputs from the team
Data sources used: The program's own registration and logging records
Public data sources?: The programme is free to join. Nothing published says whether the participation records can be obtained or on what terms, so the research group at CQUniversity would have to be asked. Note the records count sign-ups rather than the population, so they cannot be read as a participation rate.
Scale: A national participant base, run from Queensland since 2001
Key attributes: Participant registrations, steps logged, workplace and team challenge records

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics. National Nutrition and Physical Activity Survey. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2023
Task described: Measures physical activity with an accelerometer rather than asking about it, alongside diet and sleep, in the same national sample. Fills a gap the self-reported National Health Survey leaves.
Metrics / indicators: Fruit and vegetable intake against the dietary guidelines, energy and discretionary food intake, device-measured physical activity and inactivity, sleep duration and quality
Geographic level: National only. Excludes very remote areas and discrete Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities
Input data: Interviews and a 24-hour dietary recall across the sample, plus an accelerometer worn for seven days by volunteers aged 5 and over, who were 39.3 per cent of respondents
Output: National summary tables and downloadable data files by topic; microdata for approved users
Data sources used: The survey itself
Public data sources?: Summary tables and data files are free. Detailed microdata is via ABS DataLab, which charges (see the National Health Survey row for current DataLab pricing).
Scale: A national sample aged 2 and over, excluding very remote areas; the previous survey in 2011-12 sampled about 9,500 households
Key attributes: The 2023 survey uses an accelerometer instead of the pedometer used in 2011-12. It reports time spent active and asleep, but not whether adults or children meet the guidelines. The figures for children come from a separate part of the survey based on self-reported answers.
Indicators: Fruit intake; Vegetable intake; Children meeting PA guidelines; Discretionary food intake; Sugar-sweetened beverage intake

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2024). Physical activity. Canberra: AIHW web article
Task described: Publishes the national figure for how many people meet the physical activity guidelines, and how that has moved over time. The number a business case would quote.
Metrics / indicators: Share of adults and of young people meeting the physical activity guidelines, with trends
Geographic level: National, with remoteness breakdowns
Input data: Australian Bureau of Statistics health surveys
Output: National and breakdown figures against each part of the guidelines
Data sources used: ABS National Health Survey and related collections
Public data sources?: Free web article, no registration. It reports figures rather than releasing the records behind them, which come from the ABS surveys already in this scan.
Scale: National
Key attributes: Reports an improvement: 46 per cent of adults did not meet the guidelines in 2022, down from 65 per cent in 2017-18. Among young people the picture is worse, with 83 per cent of adolescents aged 15 to 17 not meeting the physical activity component in 2022
Indicators: Adults meeting PA guidelines; Children meeting PA guidelines

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2026). Overweight and obesity. Canberra: AIHW web report
Task described: Publishes how many Australians are living with overweight or obesity, and how much ill health it causes. Recent enough to quote, which most obesity figures are not.
Metrics / indicators: Share of adults and children living with overweight or obesity, and abdominal obesity
Geographic level: National, broken down by Primary Health Network, remoteness and socioeconomic area
Input data: Australian Bureau of Statistics health surveys with measured height, weight and waist
Output: National prevalence figures for adults and children, with trends
Data sources used: ABS health survey collections
Public data sources?: Free web report, no registration. Figures only; the measured records stay with the ABS.
Scale: National
Key attributes: In 2022-24 around 2 in 3 adults (67 per cent) lived with overweight or obesity, and around 1 in 4 children aged 2 to 17 (27 per cent). Abdominal obesity rose from 41 per cent in 2017-18

Reference: Baum F, Lawless A, Delany T, Macdougall C, Williams C, Broderick D, et al. (2014). Evaluation of Health in All Policies: concept, theory and application. Health Promotion International 29(suppl 1):i130-i142
Task described: Evaluates South Australia's attempt to make health everyone's business across government, not just the health department. The closest Australian precedent for what this application is trying to set up, and it says plainly what was hard.
Metrics / indicators: Not measures - the conditions that make cross-portfolio work hold together, including central agency backing and a shared mandate
Geographic level: State government
Input data: Interviews, documents and case studies from the South Australian program
Output: A framework for evaluating cross-government health work, and findings on what sustained it
Data sources used: Program documents and interviews
Public data sources?: Journal article; check for access. It is guidance rather than data.
Scale: One state's whole-of-government program
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Corbin JH, Jones J, Barry MM (2016). What makes intersectoral partnerships for health promotion work? A review of the international literature. Health Promotion International 33(1):4-26
Task described: Pulls together what is known about why partnerships between health, councils and other sectors succeed or fall apart. Directly answers this application's question about coordination, with evidence rather than assertion.
Metrics / indicators: Not measures - the factors to assess a partnership against
Geographic level: Not applicable
Input data: Published studies of intersectoral health promotion partnerships
Output: The recurring factors: shared purpose, trust, clear roles, resourcing, and leadership that survives staff turnover
Data sources used: Published literature
Public data sources?: Journal article; check for access. Guidance rather than data.
Scale: An international review
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Alderwick H, Hutchings A, Mays N (2024). Cross-sector collaboration to reduce health inequalities: a qualitative study of local collaboration between health care, social services, and other sectors under health system reforms in England. BMC Public Health 24:2613
Task described: Recent evidence on what actually happens when a health system is reorganised to make local partnership compulsory. Useful as a caution: the paper finds the structures were created but the money and the power stayed where they were.
Metrics / indicators: Not measures - what to watch for when setting up joint arrangements
Geographic level: Local health and care systems
Input data: Interviews with people running local partnerships under England's health system reforms
Output: Findings on the gap between partnership structures on paper and what changes on the ground
Data sources used: Interview data
Public data sources?: Open access paper. Guidance rather than data.
Scale: Local systems across England
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics. Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA). Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: Links health, tax, education, welfare and census records for the same people, so a question like 'did this program change hospital use' can actually be answered. It is the mechanism behind most Australian work that follows people across services.
Metrics / indicators: Whatever the linked collections hold - Medicare, pharmaceuticals, hospital, income, education, welfare
Geographic level: Person level, reportable at small area
Input data: Commonwealth administrative collections linked at person level, without names
Output: Analysis run inside a controlled environment; results are checked before release
Data sources used: Census, Medicare, Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, hospital, tax, social security and education collections
Public data sources?: Not public. Access takes a formal application, an approved project, and analysis inside the ABS environment rather than on your own machine. Slow and demanding, but it is the only route to person-level linkage at this scale.
Scale: The Australian population, linked across collections
Key attributes: Linked person records across health, income, education and welfare
Topics: Regional partnerships; Health system impact; Health inequities

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics. The Five Safes framework. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: The vocabulary Australian agencies use when deciding whether data can be shared: is the project safe, the people, the setting, the data, the output. If this project ends up asking for data it does not hold, this is the language the answer will come back in.
Metrics / indicators: Safe projects, safe people, safe settings, safe data, safe outputs
Geographic level: Not applicable
Input data: Not applicable
Output: A five-part test applied to any proposed data access
Data sources used: Not applicable
Public data sources?: The framework is published free. It is a method for deciding access, not data.
Scale: Applies to any data-sharing request
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Office of the National Data Commissioner. The Data Availability and Transparency scheme. Canberra: Australian Government
Task described: The legal route by which Australian Government data can be shared with state bodies and researchers, and the register of who is accredited to receive it. Relevant because it sets what an agency can lawfully ask for and on what terms.
Metrics / indicators: Not applicable
Geographic level: National
Input data: Not applicable
Output: Accreditation, registered data-sharing agreements, and published guidance
Data sources used: Not applicable
Public data sources?: The scheme, its guidance and the register of data-sharing agreements are public. It governs access rather than holding data itself.
Scale: Commonwealth data sharing
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. AIHW data by geography. Canberra: AIHW
Task described: A single index of which national health collections are published at which geographic level. Worth having because the recurring question in this scan is not whether a figure exists but whether it exists for a council-sized area.
Metrics / indicators: Varies by collection
Geographic level: Indexes national collections by their available geography
Input data: AIHW's own catalogue of collections
Output: A guide to what is available at Primary Health Network, Statistical Area Level 3, local government area and remoteness levels
Data sources used: AIHW collections
Public data sources?: Free, no registration. It is a finding aid rather than data.
Scale: National collections
Key attributes: Collection name against available geographic levels
Geo tags: PHN; LGA; Small area; Remoteness; National
Topics: Regional partnerships; Local government measurement; Health system impact

Reference: Australian Government. data.gov.au, the national open data portal. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: The national counterpart to the Queensland portal already in this scan. Where federal, state and local agencies publish open data, so it is the first place to look before asking an agency directly.
Metrics / indicators: Varies entirely by dataset
Geographic level: Varies by dataset, from national to street level
Input data: Whatever agencies choose to publish
Output: Dataset records with links, licences and contacts
Data sources used: Federal, state and local government agencies, plus some publicly funded research data
Public data sources?: Free to browse, no registration. The portal says 'Anyone can access the public data published by federal, state and local agencies', but not everything listed is downloadable: it also carries records for unpublished data and for data available for purchase. Individual datasets carry their own licences.
Scale: All levels of Australian government
Key attributes: The organisations that publish each dataset remain responsible for its quality and timeliness. Some files are uploaded to data.gov.au, while other listings link to data held elsewhere. Being listed does not always mean the data is free to download

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. METEOR, the Metadata Online Registry. Canberra: AIHW
Task described: The official record of how national health indicators are defined and calculated. Directly useful when deciding the exact wording of a measure, so two agencies counting the same thing count it the same way.
Metrics / indicators: Definitions rather than values: how each indicator is worded, what it counts and who registered it
Geographic level: National standards
Input data: Metadata submitted and registered by health and welfare agencies
Output: Data set specifications, indicator sets, data quality statements and data dictionaries, downloadable as CSV
Data sources used: Registered metadata from AIHW and partner agencies
Public data sources?: Free to browse and search, no registration for the public content. Some reporting outputs need a sign-in. It holds definitions, not data.
Scale: National health and welfare metadata
Key attributes: Has indicator sets and data set specifications as separate categories, which is the distinction between a named measure and the collection it is drawn from

Reference: Healthdirect Australia. National Health Services Directory. Sydney: Healthdirect Australia
Task described: A geocoded list of health services across Australia. Turns questions about whether people can reach a service into something measurable, by putting every service on a map.
Metrics / indicators: Service location, type and availability
Geographic level: Individual service addresses nationally
Input data: Service records maintained by the providers themselves and by state health departments
Output: A searchable directory, and a geocoded dataset for research through AURIN
Data sources used: Provider and health department registrations
Public data sources?: Two different things. Anyone can search the public Healthdirect service finder for free. The geocoded dataset is separate: AURIN lists it as a restricted dataset needing an application, and whether that route carries a cost is not stated on either site.
Scale: Health services nationally
Key attributes: Providers register and maintain their own entries, so coverage depends on services keeping their listing current

Reference: World Health Organization (2013). Handbook on health inequality monitoring: with a special focus on low- and middle-income countries. Geneva: World Health Organization
Task described: The standard method text for this topic's core task: how to monitor health inequalities step by step
Metrics / indicators: Simple difference and ratio between groups; slope index of inequality and relative index of inequality (which measure the gradient across all groups, not just the extremes); concentration index
Geographic level: Any level - the method applies anywhere
Input data: Health data broken down by wealth, education, sex, region and other population characteristics
Output: A monitoring framework: choose indicators, choose the population splits, calculate summary measures, report the results
Data sources used: Household surveys and routine administrative records
Public data sources?: Not a dataset

Reference: Marmot M, Allen J, Boyce T, Goldblatt P, Morrison J (2020). Health Equity in England: The Marmot Review 10 Years On. London: Institute of Health Equity / The Health Foundation
Task described: The source of 'proportionate universalism' - the targeting logic this topic asks about, meaning prevention is offered to everyone but with effort scaled up in more disadvantaged places. Also tracks a decade of inequality trends
Metrics / indicators: Gaps in life expectancy and healthy life expectancy between the most and least deprived tenths of the population
Geographic level: National down to neighbourhood
Input data: Life expectancy, death rates and social indicators from 2010 to 2020
Output: Finds inequalities widened and life expectancy stopped improving; sets out recommendations across six policy areas
Data sources used: National death and population statistics; the English Index of Multiple Deprivation (a small-area measure of disadvantage)
Public data sources?: Yes
Data sources link:
Office for National Statistics: https://www.ons.gov.uk/
Deprivation data: https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/download-all
Scale: England (2010 to about 2018-19)
Key attributes: Deprivation files: rank and decile per neighbourhood

Reference: Flavel J, Kedzior SGE, Isaac V, Cameron D, Baum F (2024). Regional health inequalities in Australia and social determinants of health: analysis of trends and distribution by remoteness. Rural and Remote Health 24:7726
Task described: The closest match in this table to this topic's core question, and it covers rural and remote Australia explicitly. The key point: differences WITHIN non-city areas are large, so regions and towns should not be lumped together when targeting prevention
Metrics / indicators: Slope index of inequality across disadvantage groups - a measure of the whole gradient, which the authors argue is better than simply comparing the most and least disadvantaged groups
Geographic level: Local government area (538 of them), grouped by how remote they are, and capital city versus rest of state
Input data: Public Health Information Development Unit data for capital cities, the rest of each state and territory, and 538 local government areas; trends from 1986 to 2018
Output: Premature and avoidable death rates fell everywhere, but the gap between richer and poorer areas WIDENED outside the capital cities; social conditions showed mixed trends
Data sources used: Public Health Information Development Unit small-area data (Torrens University); Australian Bureau of Statistics disadvantage rankings; death and census records

Reference: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care and Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2021). The Fourth Australian Atlas of Healthcare Variation. Sydney: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care. ISBN 978-1-922563-06-4
Task described: Maps healthcare use and preventable hospitalisation by small area, split by disadvantage, remoteness and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status. Chapter 2 covers preventable hospitalisations. Notes a key gap: Indigenous status is missing from Medicare and pharmaceutical data, and undercounted in hospital data
Metrics / indicators: Rates per 100,000 people adjusted for age and sex; 'magnitude of variation', meaning the highest area rate divided by the lowest. Chronic lung disease varies 18.1-fold between areas, and is 4.8 times higher for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
Geographic level: Statistical Area Level 3 (about 30,000-130,000 people); also grouped by Primary Health Network, state, remoteness and disadvantage
Input data: Hospital records 2014-15 to 2017-18; Medicare and pharmaceutical records 2018-19; birth records 2017; population estimates as denominators
Output: Maps and tables of standardised rates by small area for 18 clinical items, each with equity breakdowns. Chapter 2 covers 330,000+ preventable hospitalisations in 2017-18 across five conditions
Data sources used: National Hospital Morbidity Database; Medicare Benefits Schedule; Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme; National Perinatal Data Collection; population, remoteness and disadvantage classifications
Public data sources?: No - underlying records are not released

Reference: Canadian Institute for Health Information (2018). In Pursuit of Health Equity: Defining Stratifiers for Measuring Health Inequality - A Focus on Age, Sex, Gender, Income, Education and Geographic Location. Ottawa: Canadian Institute for Health Information
Task described: Answers this topic's 'what data is missing' question: it standardises WHICH population characteristics should be recorded alongside health data so that fair comparisons are possible
Metrics / indicators: Definitions of each population split, and the equity gap measured for each
Geographic level: National and provincial
Input data: A review of existing Canadian health databases, checking which population characteristics they capture
Output: Recommended standard definitions for six population characteristics, plus guidance on building them into data collection
Data sources used: Canadian administrative health data linked to census records
Public data sources?: No for the health records

Reference: Flanagan BE, Gregory EW, Hallisey EJ, Heitgerd JL, Lewis B (2011). A Social Vulnerability Index for Disaster Management. Journal of Homeland Security and Emergency Management 8(1), Article 3
Source type: Peer-reviewed, plus a government data tool
Task described: A widely reused composite index for identifying vulnerable areas - a working model for how Queensland could build its own index to target prevention
Metrics / indicators: A percentile ranking per theme plus an overall ranking (so an area can be placed against all others)
Geographic level: Census tract (roughly neighbourhood size)
Input data: United States census and community survey variables
Output: A vulnerability ranking for every small area, across four themes: social and economic position, household composition, ethnicity and language, and housing and transport
Data sources used: United States Census Bureau American Community Survey
Public data sources?: Yes - the index files are free to download, no registration
Data source year(s): 2000 Census in the paper; the index is published to 2022

Reference: Atkinson J, Salmond C, Crampton P, Viggers H, Lacey K (2024). NZDep2023 Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation: Research Report. Wellington: University of Otago
Task described: A small-area disadvantage index used routinely in New Zealand to allocate health funding and target services - a proven mechanism for turning disadvantage data into prevention resourcing
Metrics / indicators: The nine variables combined into a single score, then sorted into ten equal groups from 1 (least disadvantaged) to 10 (most disadvantaged)
Geographic level: Small area (roughly a few hundred people), which can be added up to any larger level
Input data: Nine variables from the 2023 census covering eight aspects of disadvantage: income, employment, communication, support, qualifications, home ownership, living space and dry housing
Output: A disadvantage score and rank for every small area in New Zealand
Data sources used: New Zealand Census of Population and Dwellings 2023
Public data sources?: Yes for the finished index
Scale: ~32,000 small areas covering all of New Zealand, generally 100-200 residents each
Key attributes: Nine census variables (income, employment, communication, support, qualifications, home ownership, space, damp housing), combined into one score reported as deciles 1-10

Reference: Maiam nayri Wingara Indigenous Data Sovereignty Collective and Australian Indigenous Governance Institute (2018). Indigenous Data Sovereignty Communique, Indigenous Data Sovereignty Summit, 20 June 2018, Canberra
Task described: Speaks to how inequity can be reported responsibly: it asserts Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' rights over how data about them is created, accessed and interpreted, countering the negative framing that can itself entrench disadvantage
Metrics / indicators: Not applicable - these are criteria to apply when choosing and reporting equity indicators
Geographic level: All levels
Input data: Not applicable - these are governance principles that apply to any Indigenous data
Output: A statement of Indigenous data sovereignty rights and data governance principles
Data sources used: Applies to all datasets about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples

Reference: Public Health Information Development Unit (PHIDU). Social Health Atlas of Australia. Adelaide: Torrens University Australia
Task described: Brings health, social and economic figures for small areas together in one place so differences between areas can be seen side by side. It is the usual starting point in Australia for asking which areas are worse off and on what.
Metrics / indicators: Chronic disease, health risk factors, socioeconomic position, and use of health services, with separate sets for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations, older people, and children and young people
Geographic level: Local government area, Primary Health Network, Statistical Area Level 3, and Population Health Area
Input data: Census, administrative health collections and national surveys, compiled per area
Output: Downloadable spreadsheets and maps, one workbook per geographic structure
Data sources used: Australian Bureau of Statistics collections, Medicare and other administrative health data, national surveys
Public data sources?: Free Excel workbooks, no registration. Attribution conditions apply - check the copyright page before republishing anything.
Scale: All of Australia at small-area level
Key attributes: One row per area, one column per indicator, with the Australian rate alongside for comparison
Topics: Health inequities; Local government measurement; Regional environments

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2023). Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA), Australia, 2021. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: Ranks every area in Australia by social and economic disadvantage, from census answers. It is what most Australian work means when it says 'the most disadvantaged areas', so using it makes results comparable with everyone else's.
Metrics / indicators: Four indexes: Relative Socio-economic Disadvantage; Relative Socio-economic Advantage and Disadvantage; Economic Resources; and Education and Occupation. Each is reported as a score, a rank, a decile and a quintile.
Geographic level: Statistical Area Level 1 and 2, local government area, and larger areas
Input data: Census variables covering income, education, employment, occupation, housing and other household characteristics
Output: A score and a rank for every area, with areas also sorted into tenths and fifths
Data sources used: Census of Population and Housing 2021
Public data sources?: Free Excel downloads, no registration.
Scale: Every area in Australia, rebuilt after each census
Key attributes: Index score, national and state rank, decile and quintile per area

Reference: Australian Longitudinal Study on Women's Health (ALSWH). Universities of Newcastle and Queensland, funded by the Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing (ongoing since 1996)
Task described: Follows four cohorts of Australian women, born 1921-26, 1946-51, 1973-78 and 1989-95, with a survey about every three years, to see how health and its causes change across a lifetime and differ between groups. One dataset behind many papers, rather than a single study.
Metrics / indicators: Self-reported health, health behaviours, use of services, reproductive and social circumstances, followed over time
Geographic level: Individual respondents nationally; area of residence held by the study rather than published
Input data: Postal and online surveys of more than 57,000 women, with consent to link Medicare, hospital and other administrative records
Output: Survey datasets by cohort and wave, plus linked administrative data on application
Data sources used: The study's own surveys; linked Medicare, Pharmaceutical Benefits and state hospital records for approved projects
Public data sources?: Application to the ALSWH Data Access Committee. No charge for a data request; a project using linked data from outside Brisbane or Newcastle should budget for travel or remote access. Commercial use is not permitted.
Scale: Over 57,000 women in four cohorts. First surveys in 1996: 14,247 (1973-78), 13,714 (1946-51), about 12,500 (1921-26); the 1989-95 cohort recruited 17,009 in 2013
Key attributes: Latest completed surveys: 1946-51 cohort survey 10 in 2022 (7,159 responses), 1989-95 cohort survey 7 in 2023 (6,335), 1973-78 cohort survey 10 in 2024 (5,789)

Reference: Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey. Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, University of Melbourne, for the Department of Social Services (ongoing since 2001)
Task described: A household panel that interviews every member aged 15 and over of the same households each year, so income, work, family and health can be followed for the same people across two decades.
Metrics / indicators: Income, employment, housing, family circumstances, and health including the SF-36 health survey and the K10 psychological distress scale
Geographic level: Individual and household, nationally; finer area detail only in the restricted release
Input data: Annual interviews and self-completion questionnaires with about 17,000 people in a nationally representative household sample
Output: A general release and a restricted release, each covering every wave to date
Data sources used: The survey itself
Public data sources?: Application through the Australian Data Archive, with a signed undertaking. No cost. Restricted release needs a further application.
Scale: About 17,000 respondents a year; 24 waves, 2001 to 2024, in release 24
Key attributes: One row per person per wave, linkable across waves; household and family identifiers
Indicators: Psychological distress; Self-rated health

Reference: Growing Up in Australia: the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC). Department of Social Services with the Australian Institute of Family Studies (ongoing since 2004)
Task described: Follows two cohorts of children recruited in 2004, one from infancy and one from age four to five, through childhood into adulthood, to show how early circumstances shape later health and wellbeing.
Metrics / indicators: Child development, physical and mental health, education, family and neighbourhood circumstances
Geographic level: Individual children nationally
Input data: Interviews and questionnaires with parents, teachers and the children themselves every two years, plus a one-off physical health assessment at ages 11 to 12
Output: Wave-by-wave datasets for both cohorts, ten main waves by 2024
Data sources used: The study itself; linked administrative data for approved projects
Public data sources?: Application through the Australian Data Archive with a project description and a deed of confidentiality. No cost.
Scale: Two cohorts recruited in 2004: 5,107 infants and a kindergarten cohort aged four to five; ten waves, the latest collected across 2023 and 2024 and released in October 2025
Key attributes: One row per child per wave with parent, teacher and child reports

Reference: Footprints in Time: the Longitudinal Study of Indigenous Children (LSIC). Department of Social Services (ongoing since 2008)
Task described: Follows about 1,700 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and their families from 2008, across urban, regional and remote areas, to learn what helps children grow up strong.
Metrics / indicators: Child health and development, social and emotional wellbeing, culture and connection to Country, family and community circumstances
Geographic level: Individual children in eleven sites chosen to span urban, regional and remote Australia
Input data: Annual interviews with the child's main carer and, as they grow, the children themselves, by Indigenous interviewers
Output: Annual waves. What can be obtained lags collection: the latest archived release covers waves 1 to 14, while interviewing has reached wave 18
Data sources used: The study itself
Public data sources?: Application through the Australian Data Archive with a signed undertaking. No cost. Use is bound by the study's Indigenous data protocols, including consultation on publication.
Scale: Two age groups recruited in 2008, aged 6 to 18 months and 3.5 to 5 years; about 1,700 children
Key attributes: One row per child per wave; site and remoteness of residence. Collection reached wave 18 in 2025, but the newest release in the archive covers waves 1 to 14, so plan around the release rather than the fieldwork

Reference: Building a New Life in Australia (BNLA): the Longitudinal Study of Humanitarian Migrants. Department of Social Services with the Australian Institute of Family Studies, 2013 to 2023
Task described: Follows humanitarian migrants who arrived or were granted permanent visas in 2013, to see what helps or hinders settlement, including physical and mental health.
Metrics / indicators: Settlement, housing, employment, English, health and mental health including post-traumatic stress
Geographic level: Individual and household, nationally
Input data: Interviews with 2,399 adults from 1,509 migrating units in wave 1, face to face and by telephone, in the respondent's own language where needed
Output: Six waves of data: five annual waves 2013-14 to 2018, then a sixth in 2023
Data sources used: The study itself
Public data sources?: Application through the Australian Data Archive with a signed undertaking. No cost.
Scale: 2,399 respondents in wave 1 (October 2013 to March 2014); 1,223 in wave 6 (January to July 2023)
Key attributes: One row per person per wave; adult, youth and child questionnaires

Reference: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (2022). Australia's children. Canberra: AIHW web report
Task described: Brings together how Australian children are faring across health, education, safety and family circumstances, so differences between groups of children can be seen in one place.
Metrics / indicators: Child health, development, education, safety and family circumstances
Geographic level: National, with population-group breakdowns
Input data: Survey, administrative and registry collections about children
Output: Indicator-by-indicator national figures with breakdowns by population group
Data sources used: ABS and AIHW collections, education and homelessness data
Public data sources?: Free web report, no registration. Published figures only.
Scale: National
Key attributes: An older broad source: the written summaries are from December 2019 and only some tables were refreshed in February 2022, so any figure should be checked against a newer release before it is quoted
Data source year(s): Varies by indicator; summaries published December 2019, tables updated February 2022

Reference: Higgs C, Badland H, Simons K, Knibbs LD, Giles-Corti B (2019). The Urban Liveability Index: developing a policy-relevant urban liveability composite measure and evaluating associations with transport mode choice. International Journal of Health Geographics 18:14
Task described: How to build and test a liveability index that is detailed enough to guide policy - the method this topic would follow
Metrics / indicators: The overall liveability score and each of its component measures
Geographic level: Individual street addresses, which can be added up to larger areas
Input data: Liveability measures calculated for every residential address in Melbourne: walkability, transport, open space, employment, housing affordability and community facilities
Output: A combined liveability score for each address, checked against how people actually travel
Data sources used: Census and disadvantage data; a Victorian travel survey; mapped infrastructure data
Public data sources?: Yes
Scale: The survey is conducted throughout the year across greater Melbourne, and periodically in Geelong and other key regional centres. Over 32,000 households contributed to this survey since 2012
Key attributes: Travel survey comes as six linked files: households, persons, trips, stops, journey to work, journey to education
Indicators: Walkability Index; Street connectivity; Dwelling density; Daily living destination index; Public transport accessibility; Green space access; % dwellings within 400m open space; Supermarket access; Housing affordability
Data source year(s): 2011 Census and the 2012 to 2014 Victorian travel survey

Reference: Higgs C, Lowe M, Hooper P, Mavoa S, Arundel J, Gunn L, Simons K, Giles-Corti B (2023). Policy relevant health related liveability indicator datasets for addresses in Australia's 21 largest cities. Scientific Data 10:113
Task described: Publishes the underlying liveability datasets as free open data - so an agency could calculate these indicators itself rather than paying for dashboard access
