Metrics / indicators: Neighbourhood liveability and access-to-amenity measures
Geographic level: Street address, which can be added up to larger areas
Input data: Built environment measures for addresses across Australia's 21 largest cities
Output: Free downloadable datasets of liveability indicators, at address level and for administrative areas
Data sources used: Census data, OpenStreetMap (a free public map), public transport timetable data and government mapping data
Public data sources?: Yes - published as open data by RMIT University. The repository blocks automated checks, so open the link in a browser
Scale: Residential address points across Australia's 21 largest cities
Indicators: Walkability Index; Street connectivity; Dwelling density; Daily living destination index; Public transport accessibility; Green space access; Supermarket access; Healthy food access; Housing affordability; Local employment

Reference: Giles-Corti B, Vernez-Moudon A, Reis R, Turrell G, Dannenberg AL, Badland H, Foster S, Lowe M, Sallis JF, Stevenson M, Owen N (2016). City planning and population health: a global challenge. The Lancet 388:2912-2924
Task described: Identifies eight city-planning levers that together encourage walking, cycling and public transport - the reasoning that links this topic's indicator areas to actual health outcomes
Metrics / indicators: The eight planning levers, and their links to chronic disease and road trauma
Geographic level: City and neighbourhood
Input data: A global review of evidence on city form, transport and health
Output: A framework plus supporting evidence for the eight planning levers
Data sources used: Published studies from many countries

Reference: Boeing G, Higgs C, Liu S, Giles-Corti B, Sallis JF, Cerin E, et al. (2022). Using open data and open-source software to develop spatial indicators of urban design and transport features for achieving healthy and sustainable cities. Lancet Global Health 10(6):e907-e918
Task described: A reusable, freely available process for calculating comparable indicators within and between cities - the template for a framework that could scale across Queensland
Metrics / indicators: Walkability; access to fresh food, public transport and open space; whether planning policy targets are being met
Geographic level: Small grids and neighbourhoods within each city
Input data: Free public map data, public transport timetable data, and official population maps
Output: Indicators for 25 cities, allowing comparison both within a city and between cities
Data sources used: Entirely free and public data sources, processed with freely available software
Public data sources?: The toolkit is open source
Scale: 25 diverse cities in 19 countrie
Key attributes: Population and street density, street connectivity, walkability, and distance to fresh food, shops, public transport and open space
Indicators: Walkability Index; Street connectivity; Dwelling density; Public transport accessibility; Green space access; Healthy food access
Data source year(s): 2015 population and urban boundaries; map extract date in the appendix

Reference: Lowe M, Whitzman C, Badland H, Davern M, Aye L, Hes D, Butterworth I, Giles-Corti B (2015). Planning Healthy, Liveable and Sustainable Cities: How Can Indicators Inform Policy? Urban Policy and Research 33(2):131-144
Task described: Directly answers this topic's design question: what makes indicators actually get picked up and used by decision-makers
Metrics / indicators: Criteria for choosing and using indicators
Geographic level: City and local government area
Input data: A review of Australian and international liveability indicator systems, plus interviews with academics and decision-makers
Output: Recommendations for making indicators policy-relevant: match them to the levers government actually controls, report them at a useful geographic detail, and communicate them well
Data sources used: Existing indicator systems; stakeholder interview data

Reference: Gourevitch MN, Athens JK, Levine SE, Kleiman N, Thorpe LE (2019). City-Level Measures of Health, Health Determinants, and Equity to Foster Population Health Improvement: The City Health Dashboard. American Journal of Public Health 109(4):585-592
Source type: Peer-reviewed, plus a live public dashboard
Task described: A mature working example of what this topic is aiming at: standardised local health measures delivered to city governments to prompt action
Metrics / indicators: Measures covering health outcomes, social and economic conditions, health behaviours, physical environment and clinical care
Geographic level: City and census tract (roughly neighbourhood size)
Input data: National health surveys, birth and death records, and federal administrative data
Output: A web dashboard of 37 measures across five areas for the 500 largest United States cities, at both city and neighbourhood level (the live version has since grown)
Data sources used: Census and community survey data; national disease control data; environmental agency data; birth and death records

Reference: Topp CW, Ostergaard SD, Sondergaard S, Bech P (2015). The WHO-5 Well-Being Index: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Psychotherapy and Psychosomatics 84(3):167-176
Task described: Evidence on whether the five-question WHO-5 wellbeing measure actually works. This is exactly the 'is this measure valid and reliable' test this topic calls for, and the measure is already in use on Queensland indicator lists
Metrics / indicators: The WHO-5 score (five questions); how well it detects what it is meant to detect; how responsive it is to change
Geographic level: Individual people, which can be added up to any area
Input data: Studies that used the five-question WHO-5 wellbeing questionnaire, in both clinical and general population settings
Output: Finds the measure performs well both for screening and for tracking change over time, and works across many different settings
Data sources used: Survey data collected in the reviewed studies
Public data sources?: No primary dataset; questionnaire free to use
Indicators: WHO-5 wellbeing score

Reference: Lytle LA, Sokol RL (2017). Measures of the food environment: A systematic review of the field, 2007-2015. Health & Place 44:18-34
Task described: Assesses whether measures of the local food environment are actually reliable - directly relevant to healthy eating indicators such as outlet density, supermarket access and the cost of a healthy food basket
Metrics / indicators: Counts of food outlets and how close they are; in-store audits; the costed healthy food basket; survey questions about how people perceive their local food options
Geographic level: Neighbourhood and small area
Input data: Studies published between 2007 and 2015 that measured food environments
Output: A critique of measurement quality across the field, finding that many measures have never been properly tested for reliability or accuracy
Data sources used: Business listings mapped geographically, in-store audit tools, and survey measures
Public data sources?: Not  a dataset
Indicators: Healthy food outlet density; Healthy food access; Healthy food basket affordability

Reference: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development & European Commission Joint Research Centre (2008). Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators: Methodology and User Guide. Paris: OECD Publishing
Task described: The standard method text for this topic's goal of a combined index or dashboard: how to weight and combine indicators, and how to test whether the result holds up
Metrics / indicators: Ways to put indicators on a common scale and weight them; techniques for checking how sensitive the final ranking is to those choices
Geographic level: Any
Input data: Any set of candidate indicators intended to be combined into a single score
Output: A ten-step framework, from setting out the underlying concept through to presenting and publishing the results
Data sources used: Applies to whatever indicator set the user supplies

Reference: Queensland Health. Preventive health survey series and the Queensland survey analytic system (QSAS). Brisbane: Queensland Health (ongoing series)
Task described: Queensland's own repeated telephone survey of adults and children, reporting how many people meet health guidelines and how that differs between parts of the state. This is the closest thing in the scan to a ready-made Queensland answer for a council-sized area, and the only source here that reports at local government area, Hospital and Health Service and Primary Health Network at once.
Metrics / indicators: Adults: overweight and obesity, daily smoking, physical activity, fruit and vegetable intake, alcohol, sunburn and sun protection. Children: the equivalent child indicators.
Geographic level: Queensland, Hospital and Health Service, Primary Health Network and local government area for adults; Queensland, Hospital and Health Service and Primary Health Network for children
Input data: Telephone interviews with a random sample of Queensland residents. Regional figures pool two survey years together so the numbers are large enough to report.
Output: Percentages by region and by sociodemographic group, through an interactive viewer, plus spreadsheets on the Queensland open data portal.
Data sources used: Queensland preventive health telephone survey
Public data sources?: Free, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0. Note the years do not agree between sources: the open data portal record lists adult surveys 2009-10 to 2015-16, while the Brisbane South needs assessment cites QPHS 2017-2022, so later years exist somewhere. Worth asking the agency which years they can actually get.
Data sources link: Open data portal record: https://www.data.qld.gov.au/dataset/self-reported-health-status-srhs-survey-series Interactive regional viewer (QSAS): https://public.tableau.com/app/profile/population.epidemiology/viz/QSAS_Regional_By_Region/Adult
Scale: A statewide random sample, pooled over two years for regional reporting
Key attributes: Region, age, sex and sociodemographic group, against each health indicator
Indicators: Fruit intake; Vegetable intake; Adults meeting PA guidelines; Children meeting PA guidelines
Data source year(s): 2009-10 to 2015-16 on the open data portal; later surveys to 2022 reported elsewhere

Reference: Queensland Government Statistician's Office. Queensland regional profiles and the Queensland regional database. Brisbane: Queensland Treasury
Task described: Builds a statistical profile of any Queensland region on request, including a region the user defines by combining smaller areas. It is the general-purpose background picture of a council area - who lives there, how they are employed, how the population is changing - rather than a health source.
Metrics / indicators: Population and projections, age and sex, country of birth, education, disability, long-term health conditions, employment and income, business counts, building approvals, recorded offences
Geographic level: Local government area, Statistical Area Level 2 to 4, Greater Capital City Statistical Area, state electoral district, or a custom region built from Statistical Area Level 2 pieces
Input data: Census, population estimates and projections, and administrative collections held across Queensland Government
Output: A profile report as PDF or web page. The companion regional database gives the same kind of figures as a time series that can be pulled out directly.
Data sources used: Australian Bureau of Statistics collections and Queensland Government administrative data
Public data sources?: Free and no registration. The profile tool gives finished reports rather than a data file, so it answers a question rather than feeding a calculation - use the regional database for figures you need to work with.
Scale: All of Queensland, down to suburb-sized areas
Key attributes: Demographic, social and economic characteristics per region

Reference: Australian Urban Observatory. Liveability indicators for Australian cities. Melbourne: RMIT University Centre for Urban Research
Task described: Maps liveability across Australia's larger cities and reports it back to councils and planners. It is the finished, maintained version of the liveability work already in this table as sources 1 and 2 of this application.
Metrics / indicators: Walkability, public transport access, access to supermarkets and grocers, public open space, social infrastructure, employment, housing, alcohol outlet access, and area demographics
Geographic level: Local government area, suburb and neighbourhood, across 21 Australian cities including Brisbane
Input data: The national liveability indicator datasets built from census, mapping and public transport data
Output: Interactive maps and area scores for each liveability domain
Data sources used: The Australian national liveability datasets produced by the same team
Public data sources?: Seeing the mapped data needs a paid partnership - the site's own wording is 'Become a Paid Partner to see Liveability Mapped'. Worth knowing before anyone plans around it. The underlying 2018 national liveability dataset is free and open, and is already in this table as source 2 of this application (Higgs et al. 2023), so the measures can be obtained without the subscription if someone is willing to do the processing.
Scale: 21 Australian cities
Key attributes: A score per liveability domain for each small area
Indicators: Walkability Index; Public transport accessibility; Supermarket access; Green space access

Reference: Global Observatory of Healthy and Sustainable Cities. 1000 Cities Challenge. Melbourne: RMIT University
Task described: Computes the same set of city measures the same way in every participating city, so one city can be compared against another rather than only against itself. Several Australian cities take part, Brisbane among them. The site sorts cities into those with a full report available and those still to come, and the list is loaded by script so it could not be read here - check where Brisbane sits before relying on it. The method behind it is source 4 of this application.
Metrics / indicators: Population within walking distance of public transport, fresh food and public open space; street connectivity; walkability; population density. Alongside these, policy measures covering transport, air quality, parking, cycling and walking infrastructure, and housing density rules.
Geographic level: Whole city, and smaller areas within a city
Input data: Open mapping and transport data for each city, plus a policy questionnaire completed locally
Output: A scorecard and report per city, and the spatial indicators behind them
Data sources used: OpenStreetMap and equivalent open data, plus locally completed policy scorecards
Public data sources?: The scorecards and reports are published free. What is downloadable, and on what terms, is not stated on the site - it would need an email to the team. The software and method are open, through source 4 of this application.
Scale: Around 80 cities across six continents, several of them Australian. Not every listed city has a published report yet.
Key attributes: Spatial and policy indicators per city
Indicators: Walkability Index; Street connectivity; Dwelling density; Public transport accessibility; Green space access; Healthy food access

Reference: Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Liveable Communities. Urban Liveability Checklist. Melbourne: RMIT University Centre for Urban Research
Task described: A checklist a planner works through to judge whether a place, built or proposed, supports health and wellbeing. It turns the liveability research into something someone can apply to a development without needing the data first.
Metrics / indicators: The built-environment features shown to support health and wellbeing, as a checklist rather than as scored measures
Geographic level: A single neighbourhood or development site
Input data: Local knowledge of the area being assessed
Output: A completed assessment of an area against the built-environment features the research links to health
Data sources used: Not applicable - it is applied to a place, not computed from a dataset
Public data sources?: Free PDF from the page above. It produces an assessment rather than data, so nothing is downloadable from it.
Scale: One site or neighbourhood at a time
Key attributes: Not applicable

Reference: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2022). Census of Population and Housing, 2021. Canberra: Australian Bureau of Statistics
Task described: Counts everyone in the country every five years. It matters here because it is the only source that measures how people travel to work, and how many people volunteer, for every small area in Queensland at once - two of the measures on the agency's own list that nothing else in this table covers.
Metrics / indicators: Method of travel to work, which gives active transport mode share directly; voluntary work for an organisation; unpaid domestic work and unpaid care; long-term health conditions; plus the usual population, income, housing and employment counts
Geographic level: Released down to Statistical Area Level 1, and for local government areas, suburbs and larger areas
Input data: A form completed by every household on census night
Output: Counts and cross-tabulations for any area, as downloadable packs or built to order in the online table tool
Data sources used: The census itself
Public data sources?: Free, no registration. Downloadable area packs, or build a table to order online.
Data sources link: Downloadable area packs: https://www.abs.gov.au/census/find-census-data/datapacks Build a table: https://www.abs.gov.au/websitedbs/censushome.nsf/home/tablebuilder
Scale: Every household in Australia, every five years; 2021 is the latest
Key attributes: Method of travel to work (MTWP), voluntary work (VOLWP), unpaid domestic work (DOMP), unpaid care (UNCAREP), long-term health conditions (LTHP)
Topics: Local government measurement; Health inequities; Regional environments
Indicators: Active transport mode share; Volunteering rate

Reference: Department of Transport and Main Roads. Principal cycle network, Queensland. Brisbane: Queensland Government open data portal
Task described: Maps the core cycle routes the state considers necessary for everyday bicycle travel. The baseline a council would measure new cycleway building against.
Metrics / indicators: Route alignment and extent of the principal cycle network
Geographic level: Route geometry across Queensland
Input data: Transport and Main Roads route planning
Output: Spatial files in shapefile, MapInfo, file geodatabase, KMZ and GeoPackage formats, with a metadata record
Data sources used: The department's own network planning
Public data sources?: Free download, no registration, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0. Updated on no fixed schedule.
Scale: Queensland-wide network
Key attributes: This is the planned network, not what has been built, so it measures intent rather than delivery. Comparing two releases would be needed to say what was actually added

Reference: Australian Urban Research Infrastructure Network (AURIN). Melbourne: University of Melbourne, for the Australian Government
Task described: A national platform holding thousands of cleaned, mapped datasets about cities and regions, with tools to analyse them. Saves assembling the same spatial data from a dozen agencies.
Metrics / indicators: Varies by dataset; includes urban health indicators and the geocoded national health services directory
Geographic level: Mostly small-area and council-level, varying by dataset
Input data: Datasets contributed by government, research and other bodies, cleaned and given consistent geography
Output: Access through the AURIN Data Provider, with analytical tools
Data sources used: Government agencies, research bodies and commercial partners
Public data sources?: Browsing the catalogue is open to anyone. Downloading needs an account, and a subset of datasets are marked restricted and need their own application on top of that. AURIN describes itself as supporting 'researchers, governments, not-for-profits and industry'. No page states whether a state agency pays, so the fee is unchecked.
Scale: Thousands of datasets, national coverage
Key attributes: Its value is the cleaning and the consistent geography rather than new collection, so each dataset still carries the limits of whoever collected it
